en: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Infinite Life, Volume One, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kang Sengkai of India during the Cao Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were great sages who had attained mastery of supernormal powers;

their names were: the Venerable Ajñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Saṃprati, the Venerable Bhadra-vākya, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Yaśas, and the Venerable Subhūti.
The Venerable One Endowed with [Qualities], the Venerable Ox-King, the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa,
the Venerable Gayā-Kāśyapa, the Venerable Nadī-Kāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Kapphiṇa.
The Venerable Mahāsthita, the Venerable Mahāśuddhāśaya, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra,
the Venerable Anāvaraṇa, the Venerable Oghavat, the Venerable Drḍhavasa, the Venerable Mukharāja,
the Venerable Phalavāha, the Venerable Sauratya, and the Venerable Nandika.
The Venerable Svāgata, the Venerable Rāhula, and the Venerable Ānanda were all such preeminent leaders as these.

Furthermore, he was accompanied by a multitude of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, including Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and all other bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa.
Furthermore, there were sixteen virtuous beings, including Bhadrapāla and others:

the Bodhisattva Sucintita, the Bodhisattva Śraddhāmati, the Bodhisattva Śūnyatāgata, the Bodhisattva Abhijñāpuṣpa, the Bodhisattva Prabhāśrī, the Bodhisattva Jñānottara, the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu, the Bodhisattva Śāntendriya, the Bodhisattva Praṇidhānamati, the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin, the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī, the Bodhisattva Madhyastha, the Bodhisattva Vinayacārin, and the Bodhisattva Vimukti. All of them followed the virtues of the Great Being Samantabhadra; they were endowed with the immeasurable practices and vows of all bodhisattvas, dwelt securely in all dharmas of merit, traversed the ten directions, exercised skillful means, entered the treasury of the Buddha-dharma, reached the ultimate other shore, and manifested the attainment of equal enlightenment in immeasurable worlds.

Dwelling in the Tuṣita Heaven, he extensively proclaimed the True Dharma; then, relinquishing that celestial palace, he descended by spirit into his mother’s womb and was born from her right side, whereupon he took seven steps.
Radiant light shone forth, universally illuminating immeasurable Buddha-lands in the ten directions, and the earth shook in six ways as he raised his voice and declared:
"I shall become the Unsurpassed Honored One in this world; Śakra and Brahmā shall serve me, and gods and humans shall look up to me with devotion."

He manifested proficiency in calculation, literature, archery, and charioteering; he was extensively versed in the arts and sciences and thoroughly practiced the various classics, while frequenting the rear garden to discourse on military tactics and test his skills.

While dwelling within the palace amidst sensory pleasures, he beheld old age, sickness, and death; realizing that the world is impermanent, he renounced his kingdom, wealth, and status to enter the mountains and study the Way. He sent back his carriage, white horse, jeweled crown, and necklaces, commanding them to return.
He cast aside precious and exquisite robes to don the dharma-garments, shaved off his hair and beard, and sat upright beneath a tree.
For six years he practiced with diligent austerity, acting in accordance with what was appropriate.
Manifesting within a world-system of five turbidities to accord with sentient beings, he displayed the presence of dust and grime before bathing in the golden stream.

The deity pressed down a tree branch so that he could grasp it and climb out of the pond; divine birds followed him with their wings as he proceeded to the site of enlightenment. Auspicious signs manifested to manifest his meritorious destiny.
Compassionately accepting the grass offered to him, he spread it beneath the Bodhi tree and sat cross-legged, emitting a great radiance to inform Māra of his presence.

Māra led his hosts to come and press him with trials, but [the Bodhisattva] subdued them all through the power of his wisdom, causing them to submit; he attained the subtle and wondrous Dharma and achieved supreme perfect enlightenment.

Śakra and Brahmā entreated him to turn the wheel of the Dharma; with the stride of a Buddha and the roar of a Buddha, he thundered forth: he beat the drum of the Dharma, blew the conch of the Dharma, wielded the sword of the Dharma, raised the banner of the Dharma, shook the thunder of the Dharma, flashed the lightning of the Dharma, poured down the rain of the Dharma, and performed the gift of the Dharma. Constantly awakening the worlds with the sound of the Dharma, his radiance universally illumined immeasurable Buddha-lands.
All worlds shook in six ways; the realm of Māra was completely encompassed and his palaces were shaken, such that all the Māras were struck with terror and submitted without exception.
He tore asunder the net of heterodoxy, extinguished all views, dispersed all defilements, and demolished the moats of desire.
He firmly guards the city of the Dharma and opens wide the gates of the Dharma;
he washes away defilements and reveals pure clarity;
he illuminates and harmonizes the Buddha-dharma, proclaiming and circulating the true transformation.

Entering the country to beg for alms, he obtained various abundant offerings; he stored up merit, manifested as a field of blessings, desired to proclaim the Dharma, and displayed a joyful smile, using the medicinal herbs of all dharmas to heal the three kinds of suffering.
He manifests the immeasurable merits of the bodhicitta, bestows the prediction of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas, and demonstrates parinirvāṇa to provide infinite salvation.
He eliminates all outflows, plants the roots of manifold virtues, and is fully endowed with subtle and unfathomable merit.
He travels through the lands of all Buddhas, universally manifesting the teachings of the Way; his practice is pure and free from defilement.
It is like a master illusionist who manifests various extraordinary forms—changing into male or female without exception—having mastered his craft so thoroughly that he can act according to his will.

These bodhisattvas are also like this: they study all dharmas, mastering them with thorough penetration; wherever they abide, their stability and truthfulness fail to fail to inspire transformation; they manifest universally throughout countless buddha-fields, never being arrogant or self-indulgent, but always feeling compassion for sentient beings.

All such dharmas are fully possessed; the Bodhisattva scriptures thoroughly expound their essential subtleties. His fame reaches everywhere as he guides and leads throughout the ten directions, and immeasurable Buddhas all together protect and keep him in mind.

Those who dwell where the Buddha dwells have all already attained that dwelling; those established by the Great Sage have all already been established. Each is able to proclaim the transformative teachings of the Tathāgata’s path, acting as great teachers for all bodhisattvas.

Using profound meditative concentration and wisdom, they guide and instruct all people; they penetrate the nature of all phenomena, comprehend the characteristics of sentient beings, clearly understand all lands, and make offerings to all Buddhas.
He manifested his body like a flash of lightning; well-trained in fearlessness, he thoroughly understood the nature of illusion.
He tore asunder the net of Māra and untied all fetters.
Transcending the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he attained the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Skillfully establishing expedient means, he manifests the three vehicles.
Within this, he displays parinirvāṇa for those of inferior and middling capacities; yet there is nothing done and nothing possessed, neither arising nor ceasing, as he attains the dharma of equality.

Fully accomplishing immeasurable dhāraṇīs and hundreds of thousands of samādhis, with faculties, wisdom, and vast universal tranquility, he deeply entered the Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas and attained the Buddha-Flower Adornment Samādhi.
They proclaim and expound all the sutras, abide in the gates of profound samādhi, and behold all the infinite Buddhas of the present, pervading them all in a single thought-moment.
They rescue those in extreme distress, whether they be skilled or unskilled; they discern and reveal the ultimate limit of reality, attaining the wisdom of the eloquence of all Tathāgatas.
They enter into all languages and sounds to transform and enlighten all beings, transcending all phenomena of the mundane world.
The mind constantly dwells with clarity upon the path that transcends the world, attaining sovereign mastery over all phenomena according to one's will.
One acts as an uninvited friend to all classes of sentient beings, shouldering the heavy responsibility of supporting the multitude of living things.
They uphold the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma and protect the Buddha-lineage so that it never ceases.

Arousing great compassion and pitying sentient beings, they exercise compassionate eloquence, bestow the eye of Dharma, block the three evil paths, and open the gates of goodness. They bestow the unasked-for Dharma upon the common people, just as a filial son loves and honors his parents.

Regarding all sentient beings as oneself, one crosses to the other shore in all roots of goodness and fully attains the immeasurable merits of all Buddhas, with wisdom and sagely brilliance that are inconceivable.
In this manner, immeasurable and incalculable great bodhisattvas gathered together at once.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s faculties were joyful, his countenance was pure, and his radiant features were majestic and sublime.
Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s sacred command, immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Today the World-Honored One’s faculties are joyful and serene; your countenance is pure and radiant; your majestic features are sublime, like a clear mirror reflecting images both within and without. Your dignified appearance is brilliant and transcendent beyond measure; never before have I beheld such exquisite excellence as this.”
"So be it, Great Sage! In my heart I have thought:

'Today the World-Honored One abides in the extraordinary Dharma; today the Hero of the World abides in that which Buddhas abide in; today the Eye of the World abides in the conduct of a Guide; today the Eminence of the World abides in the most supreme Path; today the Celestial Honored One practices the virtues of a Tathāgata.'"
"The Buddhas of the past, future, and present are mindful of one another; could it be that the present Buddha does not likewise mind the other Buddhas?
For what reason is his majestic spiritual power so radiant?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"What do you think, Ānanda?
Did the devas instruct you to come and question the Buddha,
or did you ask this of his majestic countenance out of your own wisdom and insight?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"There were no devas who came to instruct me; I merely asked about this matter based on what I have seen myself.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, Ānanda!
Your question is most refreshing.
You have given rise to profound wisdom and truly wondrous eloquence; out of compassion for sentient beings, you have asked about this meaning of wisdom.”

The Tathāgata, out of inexhaustible great compassion, takes pity on the three realms; for this reason he appears in the world to brilliantly expound the Way and its teachings, universally enabling all sentient beings to obtain the true benefit of the Dharma.
They are difficult to encounter and difficult to behold even in immeasurable billions of kalpas, appearing only occasionally like the auspicious *utpala* flower.
What you have now asked will bring great benefit, transforming and enlightening all devas and human beings.
“Ānanda! You should know that the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment is immeasurable; he guides and leads many, his vision of insight is unimpeded, and none can obstruct or cut it off.”
By the power of a single meal, one can maintain a lifespan for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of incalculable and immeasurable kalpas, even exceeding this.
One’s faculties remain joyful and unimpaired; one’s physical appearance does not change, and the radiance of one’s countenance remains unchanged.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s concentration and wisdom are perfected to the ultimate degree, and he has attained mastery over all dharmas.
"Ānanda, listen attentively; I shall now speak for you."
He replied,
“Indeed, I wish most earnestly to hear it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable eons ago, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world; he taught and delivered immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the Way and then enter parinirvāṇa."
Next there was a Tathāgata named Guangyuan (Far-reaching Light); next, named Yueguang (Moonlight); next, named Zhantanxiang (Sandalwood Fragrance);
next, named Shan-shanwang (King of Good Mountains); next, named Xumitianguan (Sumeru Heavenly Crown); next, named Xumidengyao (Equal Radiance of Sumeru);
next, named Yuese (Moon Color); next, named Zhengnian (Right Mindfulness); next, named Li gou (Free from Defilement); next, named Wuzhuo (Unattached).
Next is named Dragon Heaven; next is named Night Light; next is named Peaceful Brilliance Peak; next is named Immovable Ground;
next is named Lapis Lazuli Wondrous Flower; next is named Lapis Lazuli Golden Color;
next is named Golden Treasury; next is named Flame Light; next is named Flame Root; next is named Earth Seed; next is named Moon Image.
Next is named Sun-Sound; next is named Liberation-Flower; next is named Adorned Radiance; next is named Ocean-Awakening-Supernatural-Power;
next is named Water-Light; next is named Great Fragrance; next is named Free from Dust and Defilement;
next is named Renunciation of Weariness; next is named Jewel Flame; next is named Wondrous Summit; next is named...
Vīrasthita; next, named Guṇadhara-mati; next, named Ādityacandraprabha; next, named Candrasūryavaiḍūryaprabha;
next, named Anuttaravaiḍūryaprabha; next, named Agrasiras; next, named Bodhikusuma;
next, named Candraprabha; next, named Sūryaprabha; next, named Puṣpavarṇarāja.
Next is named Water-Moonlight; next is named Dispelling the Darkness of Delusion; next is named Transcending Obstructions;
next is named Pure Faith; next is named Auspicious Constellation; next is named Majestic Power; next is named Dharma-Wisdom;
next is named Crane-Sound; next is named Lion-Sound; next is named Dragon-Sound; next is named Abiding in the World.
All such Buddhas have already passed away.

At that time, there was next a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

At that time, there was a king who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, felt great joy in his heart. He immediately resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, renounced his kingdom and abdicated his throne to become a śramaṇa named Dharmākara. Possessing lofty talent, courage, and wisdom, he far surpassed all others in the world.
He went to the place where the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and praised him with these verses:
“Your radiant countenance is sublime, Your majestic power is infinite; Such blazing brilliance as yours Is without equal.”
The light of the sun, the moon, and mani-jewels, though blazing with radiant brilliance, is all eclipsed and rendered like a mass of ink.
The Tathāgata’s countenance transcends the world without peer; the great voice of Perfect Enlightenment resounds throughout the ten directions.
Precepts, learning, and diligence; samādhi and wisdom; his majestic virtue is peerless, extraordinary and rare.
With profound discernment and virtuous mindfulness, he exhausts the depths and reaches the innermost secrets of the ocean of all Buddhas' teachings, investigating them to their very limits.
Ignorance, desire, and anger—the World-Honored One is forever free from these; he is the Lion among Men, his divine virtues immeasurable.
His merit is vast and great, his wisdom profound and subtle; his radiant and majestic marks shake the trichiliocosm.
May I become a Buddha, equal to the Holy Dharma King; may I ferry beings across birth and death, such that none remain without liberation.
Through generosity, mental discipline, precepts, patience, and diligence—such as this samādhi—may wisdom be supreme.
I vow that upon attaining Buddhahood, I shall universally fulfill this aspiration,
providing great peace for all who are in fear.
I shall make offerings to all the immeasurable Great Sages, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
These various Buddhas are not as [worthy of veneration] as one who seeks the Way with firm correctness and without retreat.
Like the sands of the Ganges, the worlds of these Buddhas— and even further,
incalculable and countless lands— are all illuminated by their radiance, which pervades all these nations.
With such diligence, his majestic power is immeasurable.
He shall cause me to become a Buddha whose land is foremost, whose assembly is wondrous, and whose site of enlightenment is transcendent.
The land is like nirvana, without peer or equal; I shall take pity on them and deliver all beings.
Those born from the ten directions, their minds joyful and pure, having arrived in my land, they dwell in happiness and peace.
Fortunate am I that the Buddha’s faith and clarity serve as my true witness; I make this vow before him, exerting all my strength toward what I desire.
May the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, whose wisdom is unimpeded, always cause this Honored One to know the movements of my mind.
"Even if my body were to remain amidst all manner of suffering and poison, I would practice with diligence and endure it until the end without regret.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these verses, he addressed the Buddha, saying:"
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

I have resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. I pray that the Buddha will extensively proclaim the Dharma for me; I shall practice it and gather a pure and adorned land of immeasurable wondrous virtues as a Buddha-land, so that I may swiftly achieve perfect enlightenment in this world and uproot the very foundation of the suffering of birth and death.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"At that time, the Buddha Lokeśvararāja told the bhikṣu Dharmākara:
'As for the adornments of the buddha-lands you practice to cultivate, you shall know them yourself.'"
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"This meaning is vast and profound; it is not within my domain.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively expound upon the practices for the pure lands of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
"Having heard this, I shall practice according to these teachings to fulfill my vows.
At that time, the World-Honored King of Buddhas, knowing that the Bodhisattva Dharmākara’s lofty aspirations were profound and vast, immediately spoke a sutra for him, saying:
"Suppose there were a great ocean; if a single person were to measure it with a peck-measure, even after passing through kalpas, they might yet reach its bottom and obtain its wondrous treasures."
"If a person possesses a sincere heart and exerts themselves with diligence, seeking the Way without ceasing, they will surely achieve the fruit; what wish could they not attain?

Thereupon, the Buddha Lokeśvararāja extensively expounded for him the virtues and evils of the devas and humans, and the coarseness or excellence of the lands, across two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields, manifesting them all before him in accordance with his heart’s wishes.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s description of the adorned and purified lands, that bhikṣu beheld them all.
He gave rise to a supreme and most excellent vow; his mind was tranquil and his will was free from attachment, such that none in any world could equal him.
"For five full kalpas, he has contemplated and undertaken the pure practices for adorning his buddha-field.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is the lifespan in that buddha-land?"
The Buddha said:
"That Buddha's lifespan shall be forty-two kalpas.
At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara undertook the pure practices of two hundred and ten billion Buddhas' wondrous lands."
Having practiced in this way, he went to where that Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, stood with palms joined, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have already taken up the pure practices for the adornment of the Buddha-lands.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu, "You may speak now; you should know that this is the time."
"This shall give rise to joy for the entire assembly.
Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva practices this Dharma, and through these conditions, brings his immeasurable great vows to fulfillment.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"Please deign to listen and examine this: as I have vowed, I shall now explain it in full.
'If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any beings in my land who fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'"
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should, after the end of their lives, fall again into the three evil realms, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not all be of a true golden color, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should have differences in their physical forms and complexions, such that some are handsome and others ugly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not all know their past lives, down to knowing the events of hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not obtain the divine eye, such that they cannot see at least hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands below, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should not possess the divine ear such that they cannot hear and fully retain everything spoken by hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not possess the knowledge of others' minds—down to the point of knowing the mental thoughts of sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands—I shall not take supreme enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not possess the power of spiritual travel such that, in a single thought-moment, they cannot—at the very least—pass beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should give rise to thoughts of attachment to a self, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land should not abide in the stage of certainty and inevitably reach extinction (nirvana), may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, my radiance should have any limit, such that it does not shine upon at least hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands below, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, my lifespan should have a limit, even as short as a hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the śrāvakas in my land who are able to calculate their number—even if all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm, as pratyekabuddhas, were to join together for hundreds of thousands of kalpas to reckon and determine their total—I shall not take supreme enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the lifespan of the humans and devas in my land shall be immeasurable—except for those who, by their own original vows, have mastery over the length of their lives—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be even the sound of the name of anything unwholesome heard among the humans and devas in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions should not all praise and extol my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions who, with a sincere heart, believe in and rejoice in the desire to be born in my land—even if they have only ten recitations—and yet are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment; except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings of the ten directions who resolve their minds on Bodhi and cultivate various merits, and who with a sincere heart make a vow desiring to be born in my land—should I, at the time of their final passing, not manifest myself before them surrounded by a great multitude, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions who hear my name, fix their thoughts upon my land, plant roots of various virtues, and with a sincere heart dedicate their merit toward being born in my land, should not achieve their goal, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land do not all fully possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

"If, when I attain Buddhohood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas from other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of 'one birth remaining' (Ekajātipratibaddha)—except for those who, by their original vows, exercise sovereign power to transform others, donning the armor of great vows for the sake of sentient beings, accumulating roots of virtue to deliver all, and traveling through various Buddha-lands to cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva and making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions; [may I not attain perfect enlightenment]."
I shall transform and enlighten sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing them to establish themselves in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path;
I shall transcend the practices of all ordinary stages and manifest the cultivation of the virtues of Samantabhadra—if I do not achieve this, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the Bodhisattvas in my land, by receiving the Buddha's spiritual power, should be unable to travel in a single mealtime to immeasurable, incalculable billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands to make offerings to all Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, before the presence of all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue, yet the various requisites they seek for making offerings do not appear according to their wishes, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not be able to expound all-knowledge, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not obtain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans, devas, and all myriad things within my land shall be adorned, pure, radiant, and magnificent; their forms and colors shall be exceptionally distinguished, reaching the utmost subtlety and wonder, such that none can fathom or measure them."
"If those sentient beings, even those who have attained the divine eye, were unable to clearly discern the names and numbers [of the trees], I would not attain perfect enlightenment.

'If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land—even those of the least merit—were unable to know and see the Bodhi-tree, which possesses immeasurable light and color and rises four million li high, I would not attain perfect enlightenment.'"
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and explain the Dharma should not obtain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land should be limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land is so pure that it illuminates and reflects all the infinite, countless, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as clearly as one sees one's own face in a bright mirror;
if it were otherwise, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, from the ground up to the void of space, all things within this land—including palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, streams, flowering trees, and every other myriad object—should not be composed of countless varieties of diverse jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of incense, so marvelous and magnificent as to surpass those of all humans and devas; and if the fragrance thereof should not pervade the worlds of the ten directions such that all Bodhisattvas who smell it cultivate the practices of the Buddha, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the various classes of sentient beings in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who are touched by my radiance should not have their bodies and minds become supple and surpass those of humans and devas,
may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the various classes of sentient beings in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name should not obtain the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the various profound *dhāraṇīs*, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be women in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, rejoice with faith and delight, resolve their minds on Bodhi, and yet after the end of their lives should again take on a female form—I would not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitudes of Bodhisattvas in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should not always practice the pure life (brahmacarya) until they reach the path of Buddhahood after the end of their lives;
if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and people of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name should not prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, bowing their heads in worship, and joyfully believing and delighting in the practice of the Bodhisattva path—
such that all gods and men do not pay them respect— if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the humans and devas in my land who desire clothing should have it appear before them at the mere thought of it, and as the Buddhas have praised, such wondrous robes in accordance with the Dharma should naturally appear upon their bodies;
if there were still any need for cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the joy experienced by the humans and devas in my land should not surpass that of the bhikṣus who have exhausted their outflows, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. "If, when I attain Buddhahood,

the bodhisattvas in my land should desire to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, yet these lands were not reflected within the jeweled trees at that very moment according to their wishes—
just as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a clear mirror— may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name should not have their faculties fully perfected until they attain Buddhahood themselves, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name shall all attain the Samādhi of Pure Liberation; and while abiding in this samādhi, for the duration of a single thought-moment, they shall make offerings to immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, without losing their concentrated mind—if this be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name should not, at the end of their lives, be born into noble and honorable families;
should this not be so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from the lands of other quarters who hear my name do not leap for joy, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, and become fully endowed with the roots of virtue;
if this should not be so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of other lands who hear my name should not all attain the Samādhi of Universal Equality and, abiding in this samādhi until they achieve Buddhahood, constantly see the infinite, inconceivable Tathāgatas of all quarters;
should this not be so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
“If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should not be able to hear whatever Dharma they wish to hear according to their aspirations,
may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name do not immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression, may I not achieve perfect enlightenment."

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name do not immediately attain the first, second, or third stage of dharma-patience, or cannot immediately attain non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, after the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken these vows, he spoke in verse:
'I have established supramundane vows; I shall surely reach the Unsurpassed Way. "
If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall not attain equal enlightenment.
Throughout immeasurable kalpas, if I do not become a great donor who universally relieves all who suffer in poverty, I shall not attain equal enlightenment.
Until I have attained the path of Buddhahood, And my fame surpasses that of the ten directions,
Such that it is ultimately unheard of anywhere, I vow not to achieve equal enlightenment.
Free from desire and with profound right mindfulness, With pure wisdom, I shall cultivate the holy life.
Vowing to seek the unsurpassed path, he becomes a teacher for devas and humans.
With his supernormal powers, he manifests a great light that universally illumines boundless lands;
it eliminates the darkness of the three defilements and clearly rescues all from calamities and hardships.
Opening the eye of wisdom, extinguishing this darkness of ignorance and blindness,
blocking off all evil paths, and opening wide the gates to the happy realms;
with merit and blessings fully perfected, his majestic radiance illuminates the ten directions.
The sun and moon withdraw their layered radiance, and the light of heaven is hidden and does not appear.
For the sake of the multitude, you open the treasury of the Dharma and extensively bestow the jewels of merit;
ever amidst the great assembly, you roar the lion’s roar of the Dharma.
Making offerings to all Buddhas, Fulfilling the roots of all virtues, May wisdom be fully perfected,
And may I become a hero of the three realms.
Like the Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom, Pervading everywhere without exception, I seek to attain such thorough penetration.
May the power of my merit be equal to that of this Most Victorious Honored One.
If this vow bears fruit, may the great trichiliocosm tremble;
may the devas and humans throughout space rain down precious and wondrous flowers.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“When the Bhikṣu Dharmākara had finished reciting these verses, at that moment the entire earth shook in six ways; the heavens rained down exquisite flowers which were scattered upon it, and celestial music spontaneously arose from the air, praising him, saying:
‘He shall certainly and surely attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.’”
Thereupon, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara fully cultivated and perfected such great vows; they were sincere and true, not false, transcending the world and deeply delighting in quiescent extinction.

“Ānanda! In the presence of that Buddha, amidst the great assembly of the eight classes of beings—gods, Māras, Brahmās, nāgas, and spirits—the Bhikṣu Dharmākara made these grand vows. Having established these aspirations, he focused his mind single-mindedly on adorning a wondrous land.”
The Buddha-land he cultivates is vast and expansive, transcendent, peerless, and sublime; it is established eternally, without decay or change.

Throughout inconceivable billions of eons, he has accumulated the immeasurable virtues of a bodhisattva, never giving rise to thoughts of desire, anger, or malice, nor conceiving notions of desire, anger, or malice, and remaining unattached to the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
Having perfected the power of patience, they do not calculate the various sufferings.
With few desires and contentment, they are free from defilement, anger, and delusion; their samādhi is ever tranquil, and their wisdom is unimpeded.

Free from deceit, hypocrisy, and crookedness of mind, he maintains a serene countenance and gentle speech, anticipating others' needs to offer greetings; with courageous diligence and a will untiring, he single-mindedly seeks the pure and wholesome Dharma.
They benefit sentient beings with wisdom, revere the Triple Gem, and serve their teachers and elders;
through great adornments, they fulfill all practices, causing all sentient beings to achieve merit and virtue.
Abiding in the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—unconditioned and unarisen—one contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions.

One remains far removed from coarse speech that harms oneself, harms others, or harms both self and other; instead, one cultivates wholesome speech that benefits oneself, benefits others, and benefits both self and other.
He abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship, severing all attachment to wealth and sensual pleasures.
He personally practiced the six *pāramitās* and taught others to do likewise.

Having accumulated merit and virtue over incalculable eons, wherever he was born and according to his wishes, immeasurable treasuries of jewels spontaneously appeared in response; thus he transformed and established countless sentient beings in the Way.

Abiding in the unsurpassed, truly correct path, they may become elders, lay devotees, members of noble families, or persons of high status; or they may become Kṣatriya rulers, wheel-turning sage kings (cakravartin), or even lords of the six heavens of desire up to the Brahmā kings.
He constantly makes offerings and shows reverence to all Buddhas through the four means of support; such merit is beyond description.
His breath is fragrant and pure like the *utpala* flower, and from all the pores of his body issues the scent of sandalwood, its fragrance pervading immeasurable worlds.

His countenance is upright and handsome, his marks and signs are exceptionally sublime, and from his hands there constantly emerge inexhaustible treasures: clothing, food and drink, rare and wonderful flowers and incense, as well as various canopies, banners, pennants, and articles of adornment.
"Such matters as these transcend those of humans and devas, and he has attained mastery over all dharmas.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Has the Bodhisattva Dharmākara already attained Buddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa, or has he not yet attained Buddhahood?"
"Is he present now?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now already attained Buddhahood; he is currently in the West, a hundred thousand koṭis of lands away from here. That Buddha-world is named Sukhāvatī."
Ānanda asked again:
"How much time has passed since that Buddha attained enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
“Since he attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed.
His Buddha-land is naturally composed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate—forming its ground, which is vast, expansive, and boundless.”

They were all intermingled and interspersed with one another, radiating brilliant and dazzling light, exquisite and wondrously beautiful, pure and majestic, surpassing the finest of all the jewels in all the worlds of the ten directions; those jewels were like the precious gems of the Sixth Heaven.
Furthermore, in that land there are no Mount Sumeru, no Iron Ring Mountains, nor any other mountains; likewise, there are no great oceans, small seas, streams, channels, wells, or valleys.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, whatever one wishes to see, one sees.
Furthermore, there are no miserable realms such as those of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Nor are there the four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, and summer; it is neither cold nor hot, but always harmonious and temperate.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If that land has no Mount Sumeru, upon what do the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven depend for their dwelling?”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Upon what do the gods from the third Heaven of Heat up to the Ultimate Formlessness (Akaniṣṭha) depend for their abode?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"The retribution for karmic actions is inconceivable.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "The retribution for karmic actions is inconceivable; the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable."
"It is because those sentient beings abide in the ground of karmic action through the power of their merit and virtue that they are able to do so.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "I have no doubt regarding this Dharma; however, for the sake of future sentient beings who wish to eliminate their doubts, I have asked about this meaning."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The majestic spiritual light of Amitāyus Buddha is most honored and supreme; it cannot be equaled by the light of any other Buddhas.

While some Buddhas’ lights illuminate a hundred Buddha-worlds, or a thousand Buddha-worlds—to speak in brief—it illuminates as many Buddha-lands in the eastern direction as there are sands in the Ganges River; the same is true for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir."
There are some whose Buddha-light illuminates seven feet; some illuminate one yojana, or two, three, four, or five yojanas; thus it increases twofold until it illuminates an entire Buddha-field.

For this reason, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is named the Buddha of Immeasurable Light, the Buddha of Boundless Light, the Buddha of Unobstructed Light, the Buddha of Unrivaled Light, the Buddha of Flaming King Light, the Buddha of Pure Light, the Buddha of Joyful Light, the Buddha of Wisdom Light, the Buddha of Uninterrupted Light, the Buddha of Inconceivable Light, the Buddha of Ineffable Light, and the Buddha who Surpasses the Light of the Sun and Moon.

"Any sentient beings who encounter this light will have their three defilements extinguished; their bodies and minds will become supple, they will leap for joy, and wholesome states of mind will arise."
If those in the three miserable realms and places of diligent suffering behold this light, they shall all find rest and no longer experience affliction;
after their lives end, they shall all attain liberation.
“The radiance of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is so magnificent that it illuminates all the buddha-lands of the ten directions, such that there is none who does not hear of it or know of it.
Not only do I now extol his radiance, but all the Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the assembly of bodhisattvas likewise praise him in common.”

If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing of the merit of his radiance and majestic spiritual power, praise it day and night with an uninterrupted, sincere heart, they shall be born in that land according to their wishes. They will be praised and extolled for their merits by the great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;
and when they later attain the Way of the Buddha, all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions will likewise praise their radiance, just as they do now.
The Buddha said:

"I have spoken of the immeasurable Buddha Amitāyus’s radiance and majestic spiritual power as being so lofty and sublime that even a single kalpa of day and night would not suffice to describe them all.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"The lifespan of the Buddha Amitāyus is so long that it cannot be measured or calculated; do you truly know this?

Suppose all the immeasurable sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions were to attain human bodies, and you were to cause them all to achieve the stages of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha; then, gathering together with a single-minded focus in meditative concentration, they were to exhaust their intellectual powers to perform calculations for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas—yet they would still be unable to fathom its length or know its ultimate limit."
The lifespans of the assemblies of śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans are likewise such that they cannot be known through calculation or analogy.

Furthermore, the number of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas is immeasurable and beyond description; their spiritual wisdom penetrates all things and their sovereign power is absolute, such that they can hold all worlds within the palms of their hands.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“In that Buddha’s first assembly, the number of śrāvakas is beyond calculation, and the same is true for the bodhisattvas.

Even if one were as capable as Mahāmaudgalyāyana in calculating and comparing them for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of immeasurable and innumerable asaṃkhyeya nayuta kalpas, until even his parinirvāṇa, one could not exhaustively determine their total number.”
For example, suppose there is a great ocean, deep and vast beyond measure; if a person were to split a single hair into one hundred parts and take a single drop with one of those parts.
"What do you think?
Between those drops and that great ocean, which would be more numerous?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"The amount of water in those drops compared to the great ocean is such that it cannot be known through skillful calculation, numerology, speech, or analogies.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If those like Maudgalyāyana were to calculate the number of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in that first assembly for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas, what they could know would be like a single drop, while what they could not know would be like the waters of the great ocean."

Furthermore, in that land, trees made of the seven treasures fill the world—gold trees, silver trees, lapis lazuli trees, crystal trees, coral trees, agate trees, and musaragalva trees; some are composed of two, three, or even up to seven treasures combined together.
There were some golden trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits of silver;
some silver trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits of gold;
and some lapis lazuli trees with leaves of crystal, their flowers and fruits being likewise.
Some are crystal trees with lapis lazuli leaves, and their flowers and fruits are likewise;
some are coral trees with agate leaves, and their flowers and fruits are likewise;
some are agate trees with lapis lazuli leaves, and their flowers and fruits are likewise.
There are some *musāragalva* trees, with leaves made of various jewels, and their flowers and fruits likewise;
or there are jewel-trees with roots of purple gold, stems of white silver, branches of lapis lazuli, twigs of crystal, leaves of coral, flowers of agate, and fruits of *musāragalva*;
or there are jewel-trees with roots of white silver, stems of lapis lazuli, branches of crystal, twigs of coral, leaves of agate, flowers of *musāragalva*, and fruits of purple gold.

There were some jewel trees with lapis lazuli for their roots, crystal for their trunks, coral for their branches, agate for their twigs, musaragalva for their leaves, purple gold for their flowers, and white silver for their fruits;

there were some jewel trees with crystal for their roots, coral for their trunks, agate for their branches, musaragalva for their twigs, purple gold for their leaves, white silver for their flowers, and lapis lazuli for their fruits;

there were some jewel trees with coral for their roots, agate for their trunks, musaragalva for their branches, purple gold for their twigs, white silver for their leaves, lapis lazuli for their flowers, and crystal for their fruits.

There were some jewel trees with agate for their roots, musaragalva for their trunks, purple gold for their branches, white silver for their twigs, lapis lazuli for their leaves, crystal for their flowers, and coral for their fruits;

there were also some jewel trees with musaragalva for their roots, purple gold for their trunks, white silver for their branches, lapis lazuli for their twigs, crystal for their leaves, coral for their flowers, and agate for their fruits.

The branches met one another, the stalks faced one another, the twigs corresponded to one another, the leaves turned toward one another, the flowers accorded with one another, and the fruits matched one another; their radiant splendor was such that it could not be fully beheld.
A pure breeze blows from time to time, producing the five musical notes; the subtle and wondrous tones of *gong* and *shang* naturally harmonize with one another.

Furthermore, the Bodhi tree of Amitāyus Buddha is four million *li* high; its trunk has a circumference of five thousand *yojanas*, and its branches and leaves spread out twenty thousand *li* in all directions.
All manner of precious jewels spontaneously coalesced to form it, adorned with the moonlight-mani jewel and the ocean-wheel treasure—the king of all jewels.
Between the surrounding branches hang precious necklaces, manifesting hundreds of thousands of millions of colors and various transformations, with immeasurable rays of light shining boundlessly.
A network of exquisite, wondrous jewels covers them from above, and all manner of adornments appear in accordance with conditions.
A gentle breeze stirs, producing the sublime sounds of the Dharma that flow universally throughout all Buddha-lands in the ten directions.

Those who hear these sounds attain the profound *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the Dharma), abide in non-retrogression, and proceed until they reach the path of Buddhahood, never encountering suffering or affliction.

Whether beholding its form with the eyes, hearing its sound with the ears, perceiving its fragrance with the nose, tasting its flavor with the tongue, touching its light with the body, or contemplating it through the Dharma with the mind, all attain the most profound *dharmakṣānti*, abide in non-retrogression, and proceed until they reach the path of Buddhahood; their six sense faculties become pure and translucent, free from all distress and affliction.
“Ānanda! If the humans and devas of that land see this tree, they will attain three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*):

first, the patience of resonance (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*); second, the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*); and third, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).”
All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha Amitāyus, his power of original vows, his fulfilled vows, his clearly realized vows, his steadfast vows, and his ultimate vows.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The worldly monarchs possess hundreds of thousands of musical instruments; from the wheel-turning sage kings up to the sixth heaven, the sounds of their music increase in excellence ten thousand million times over one another.

Yet the myriad kinds of musical sounds in the sixth heaven do not equal even a single kind of sound from the trees made of the seven treasures in the Land of Immeasurable Life by ten thousand million times."

There are also ten thousand kinds of natural musical performances, and the sounds of these instruments are none other than the sounds of the Dharma—clear, resonant, plaintive, and brilliant, subtle, exquisite, and harmonious; among all sounds throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they are the most supreme.

"Furthermore, the lecture halls, monasteries, palaces, and towers were all adorned with the seven treasures, spontaneously manifested through transformation; moreover, they were covered above by canopies of pearls, moon-bright maṇi-jewels, and various precious gems."

Within and without, to the left and right, there are various bathing pools, measuring ten yojanas, or twenty, thirty, and even up to a hundred thousand yojanas; their length, breadth, and depth are each equal, filled to the brim with water of eight virtues, serene and pure, with a fragrance as clean as nectar.

The golden ponds have beds of white silver sand; the white silver ponds have beds of golden sand; the crystal ponds have beds of lapis lazuli sand; the lapis lazuli ponds have beds of crystal sand; the coral ponds have beds of amber sand; the amber ponds have beds of coral sand; the musāragalva ponds have beds of agate sand; the agate ponds have beds of musāragalva sand; the white jade ponds have beds of purple gold sand; and the purple gold ponds have beds of white jade sand—or rather, they are composed of two, three, or even up to seven precious substances combined together.
Upon the banks of that pond stood sandalwood trees, their flowers and leaves hanging down and spreading out, their fragrance wafting everywhere.
Celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses—of various colors, radiant and luxuriant—completely covered the surface of the water.
"If those bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas enter the jewel pond and wish for the water to submerge their feet, the water immediately submerges their feet;
if they wish for it to reach their knees, it immediately reaches their knees;
if they wish for it to reach their waists, the water immediately reaches their waists."
If he wished for the water to reach his neck, it would immediately reach his neck;
if he wished for it to drench his body, it would naturally drench his body;
if he wished for it to recede, the water would immediately recede.

The temperature was naturally harmonized, being neither cold nor hot; it awakened the spirit and gladdened the body, washing away the impurities of the mind until it was clear, bright, and pure as if formless.

The precious sands reflected through it all, leaving no depth unilluminated; subtle ripples circled in eddies, flowing back and forth in mutual confluence, moving with serene slowness—neither too slow nor too fast.

Boundless, spontaneous, and wondrous sounds resounded, such that there was no one who did not hear them according to their respective needs: some heard the sound of the Buddha, some the sound of the Dharma, some the sound of the Saṅgha; some heard the sound of tranquility, the sound of emptiness and non-self, the sound of great compassion, or the sound of the pāramitās; some heard the sound of the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, the sound of all-encompassing wisdom, the sound of non-action, the sound of neither arising nor ceasing, the sound of the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena, and even the sound of the various wonderful Dharmas of the nectar-anointing consecration.

Upon hearing such sounds as these, they experienced immeasurable joy. These sounds accorded with the true meaning of purity, detachment, and cessation; they accorded with the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique qualities of the Triple Gem; and they accorded with the path practiced by bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas endowed with supernormal wisdom.
There is no mention of the sufferings and hardships of the three evil realms; there is only the sound of spontaneous bliss. For this reason, that land is named "Ultimate Bliss. "Ānanda!

Those who are reborn in that Buddha-land are endowed with such pure physical bodies, wondrous voices, and the merit of supernormal powers; their palaces, clothing, food and drink, and various exquisite flowers, incenses, and ornaments are like the spontaneous objects of the Sixth Heaven.

When they wish to eat, vessels made of the seven treasures appear naturally before them; bowls of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and bright moon pearls arrive according to their wishes, spontaneously filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors.

Although there is this food, in truth there is no one who eats it; they merely see its color and smell its fragrance, and their minds take it as food, whereby they naturally become satiated, their bodies and minds become supple, and they remain free from any attachment to its flavor.
Having completed his work, he passed away; when the time arrived, he appeared once more.
"That Buddha-land is pure and peaceful, subtle and blissful, second only to the unconditioned path of Nirvana."
The śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, humans, and devas therein possess lofty and brilliant wisdom, and their supernormal powers are thoroughly penetrating.
They are all of one and the same kind, their forms being without any difference; it is only because they conform to the conventions of other regions that they bear the names "human" or "deva."

Their countenances were upright and handsome, surpassing all in the world and rare to behold; their complexions were subtle and wondrous, being neither celestial nor human, for they all possessed bodies of spontaneous non-substantiality and forms of infinite extent.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Suppose there were a poor beggar in this world standing beside a sovereign king; would his physical appearance and countenance ever be comparable [to the king's]?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

"Even if this person were to stand beside a sovereign emperor, he would be so emaciated, wretched, and hideous that no analogy could suffice; he would be a hundred thousand million billion times more so than can be calculated. Why is this? "

These impoverished beggars are the most wretched and lowly of men; their clothing does not cover their bodies, and their food barely sustains life. Suffering from hunger and cold, their human dignity is nearly extinguished.

All this is due to the fact that in previous lives they failed to plant the roots of virtue; they accumulated wealth but did not practice giving, becoming increasingly stingy as they grew rich. They desired only to obtain things for nothing, greedily seeking more without satiety, having no faith in cultivating goodness, while piling up evils like mountains.

When life thus comes to an end, wealth and treasures dissipate; though one has accumulated them through physical hardship, they become a source of grief and affliction. They benefit oneself not at all, serving only the interests of others.
Having no good deeds to rely upon and no virtues to depend on, one consequently falls into the evil realms at death and undergoes this long-lasting suffering.
When their transgressions were exhausted, they were reborn as lowly and base individuals; being the height of folly and vulgarity, they appeared outwardly like ordinary humans.

Thus, the emperors and kings of the world who are uniquely honored among men do so entirely because of the merit accumulated in past lives; through their compassion and generosity, their broad charity, their benevolence and universal succor, and their practice of faith and goodness, they remained free from all conflict and contention.
Therefore, at the end of their lives, they received the karmic response of ascending to the good paths; born above in the heavens, they enjoyed such blessings and joy.

Through the accumulated merit of past goodness, they have now attained human form, being born into a royal family where they are naturally noble and dignified. Their appearance is upright and handsome, such that all revere and serve them, and they enjoy exquisite garments and rare delicacies according to their heart's desire.
"Chased by the merit of past lives, he was thus able to achieve this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"What you say is correct."

Consider, for instance, that although an emperor is the most honored among men and possesses a handsome appearance, when compared to a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King, he appears utterly vulgar and base—just like a beggar standing beside an emperor.

The majestic appearance of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is so exceptionally sublime that it is the foremost in all the world; yet compared to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it is again a hundred thousand million times more hideous and cannot even be compared to him.
Even if one were to compare Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to the King of the Sixth Heaven, they would not be comparable by even a hundred thousand *koṭi* times.

Furthermore, if one were to compare the King of the Sixth Heaven to the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of the Land of Immeasurable Life, his radiant countenance and physical appearance would not approach theirs by hundreds of thousands of millions of *koṭis*, beyond all calculation.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In the Land of Immeasurable Life, the various devas and humans possess clothing, food and drink, flowers, incense, necklaces, parasols, banners, and pennants, as well as subtle and wondrous sounds. Their dwellings—houses, palaces, and towers—are proportionate to their respective forms, colors, heights, and dimensions; whether made of one jewel, two jewels, or even immeasurable varieties of jewels, they appear exactly as desired and arrive instantly upon thought.”
Furthermore, exquisite garments made of various jewels were spread across the ground, upon which all humans and devas tread as they walk.

Immeasurable jewel nets covered the Buddha from above, all adorned and interlaced with golden threads, pearls, hundreds of thousands of diverse gems, and wondrous, rare treasures; bells of precious stones hung around the four sides, their radiant colors shimmering in the utmost splendor and beauty.
The natural virtue of the wind arose gently and stirred subtly; its breeze was harmonious, being neither cold nor hot.
It was temperate, cool, and soft, moving neither too slowly nor too swiftly.

As it blew through the various jeweled nets and the many precious trees, it produced immeasurable and subtle sounds of the Dharma, and spread forth ten thousand kinds of refined and elegant fragrances of virtue.

Those who hear it will find that the habitual tendencies of afflictions naturally do not arise; when the wind touches their bodies, they all attain bliss, just as a bhikṣu attains the samādhi of cessation.

"Furthermore, the wind blows and scatters flowers that fill the Buddha-field; they follow their respective colors in orderly succession without being intermingled. They are soft, lustrous, and intensely fragrant. When one steps upon them, they sink down four inches, and as soon as the foot is lifted, they return to their original state."

Once the flowers have served their purpose, the ground immediately cracks open, and they vanish in succession into purity without a trace; as the seasons change, the wind blows the flowers away, and this occurs six times in such a manner.

Furthermore, lotus flowers made of various jewels fill the world; each jewel flower has hundreds of thousands of billions of petals, and the radiance of these petals is of immeasurable colors: blue petals emit blue light, white petals emit white light, and the same is true for dark-blue, yellow, crimson, and purple light. They blaze and shimmer, outshining the sun and the moon.
From each and every flower there issued forth thirty-six hundred thousand billion rays of light;
from each and every ray of light there emerged thirty-six hundred thousand billion Buddhas, their bodies the color of purple-gold, with marks and signs of excellence most extraordinary.
Each of these Buddhas further emitted hundreds of thousands of beams of light, universally preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma throughout the ten directions.
"In this way, each of these Buddhas establishes immeasurable sentient beings upon the Buddha’s true path.
*The Sutra of Immeasurable Life*, Volume One;
*The Buddha-Spoken Sutra of Immeasurable Life*, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of India during the Cao Wei Dynasty.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda: “Any sentient beings who are born in that land shall all abide in the stage of those destined for right determination.”

Why is this so? Because in that Buddha-land there are no groups of those with wrong views nor any of indeterminate nature; the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all together praise the inconceivable majestic power and meritorious virtues of Amitāyus Buddha.

All sentient beings who hear his name and rejoice with faith, even for a single thought-moment, and wholeheartedly dedicate their merit toward the vow to be born in that land, shall immediately attain rebirth there and dwell in the stage of non-retrogression—excepting only those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the True Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, there are three classes of those who, with a sincere heart, vow to be reborn in that land."

As for those of the highest grade, they leave home and renounce desire to become śramaṇas; they resolve their minds on bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha, cultivating various merits with the vow to be born in that land.

When these sentient beings approach the end of their lives, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them; they shall then be reborn in that land following that Buddha, spontaneously manifesting by transformation within lotuses made of the seven treasures, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression, possessing courageous wisdom and sovereign supernatural powers.
Therefore, Ānanda!

Any sentient beings who wish to see Amitāyus Buddha in this present life should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta), cultivate meritorious virtues, and vow to be born in that land.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"As for those of the middle grade—among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions—who possess a sincere heart and wish to be born in that land, though they cannot become śramaṇas or extensively cultivate meritorious deeds, they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively keep Amitāyus Buddha in mind."

To whatever extent one has cultivated goodness, observed the precepts and fasts, erected stupas and images, provided food for śramaṇas, hung silk banners and lit lamps, scattered flowers and burned incense—dedicating these merits with the vow to be born in that land.

When that person approaches the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha manifests a transformed body—possessing radiance and the marks and signs of excellence exactly like those of a true Buddha—and appears before them together with a great assembly. Thereupon, the person is reborn in that land following the transformed Buddha, abiding in the stage of non-retrogression; their merit and wisdom are next only to those of the superior grade.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"As for those of the lowest grade, among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, if there are those who with a sincere heart desire to be born in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi, single-mindedly and exclusively focus their intent for up to ten recitations, calling to mind Amitāyus Buddha and vowing to be born in his land."

If one hears this profound Dharma and rejoices with faith and delight, giving rise to no doubt or confusion, and even for a single moment of thought brings that Buddha to mind, then with a sincere heart they vow to be born in that land.
When this person is near death, they will see that Buddha in a dream and shall likewise attain rebirth there; their merit and wisdom will be next only to those of the middle grade.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus Buddha is infinite; throughout the ten directions, there are immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable Buddhas, Tathāgatas, who all praise him.”

In the eastern direction, across Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of bodhisattvas all proceeded to the abode of the Buddha Amitāyus to pay respectful homage and make offerings; they also listened to and received the Dharma from the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, proclaiming and transforming others through the Way.
It was likewise so in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In the Buddha-lands of the eastern direction, Their number is like the sands of the Ganges;
The Bodhisattvas of those lands Go forth to behold the Immeasurable Awakened One."
In the south, west, north, and the four intermediate directions, and likewise above and below;
the multitudes of bodhisattvas from those lands go to behold the Immeasurable Awakened One.
All these bodhisattvas each carry exquisite celestial flowers.
With precious incense and priceless robes, they make offerings to the Immeasurable Awakened One;
together they play celestial music, producing harmonious and elegant sounds,
singing praises of the Most Victorious Honored One, making offerings to the Immeasurable Awakened One.
Having thoroughly mastered supernatural powers and wisdom, he enters and dwells within the profound Dharma-gates;
possessing a treasury of merit, his wondrous knowledge is peerless.
Like the sun of wisdom shining upon the world, he dispels the clouds of birth and death.
Reverently circumambulating him three times, they bowed their heads to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Beholding that adorned and pure land, subtle and inconceivable,
they gave rise to immeasurable resolve, vowing that their own lands should likewise be so.
At that moment, the Honored One of Immeasurable Light moved his countenance and broke into a joyful smile;
from his mouth issued forth countless rays of light, which shone everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions.
These rays returned and circled his body three times before entering through the crown of his head.
All the hosts of devas and humans leaped for joy and were filled with gladness.
The Great Being Avalokiteśvara, having adjusted his robes and bowed his head,
addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason do you smile?
We pray that you will graciously declare your intention.
With a voice like the roll of thunder, he uttered the sublime resonance of the eight qualities of speech:
"I shall bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon the Bodhisattvas; listen now attentively as I speak.
These noble beings who have come from the ten directions—I know all their vows;
they seek to adorn and purify the Buddha-lands, and having received this prediction, they shall become Buddhas."
Realizing that all phenomena are like dreams, illusions, and echoes,
One fulfills all sublime vows and will surely achieve such a buddha-field.
Knowing that dharmas are like flashes of lightning, One brings the bodhisattva path to ultimate completion.
Possessing the roots of all merits, they shall receive the prophecy of future Buddhahood;
penetrating all dharma-gates— that all things are empty and without self—
they single-mindedly seek pure Buddha-lands, and will surely achieve such realms.
The Buddhas told the Bodhisattvas:
"Cause them to behold the Buddha of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), to hear the Dharma, and to joyfully accept and practice it, so that they may swiftly attain the state of purity."
Upon reaching that adorned and pure land, one will swiftly attain supernatural powers;
before the Honored One of Immeasurable Life, one will certainly receive the prediction of attaining equal enlightenment.
By the power of that Buddha’s original vow, those who hear his name and desire to be reborn there—
They all arrive in that land, personally attaining the stage of non-retrogression.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to this aspiration: "May my own land be no different from that;
may I universally resolve to deliver all beings, and may my name become renowned throughout the ten directions."
Having served billions of Tathāgatas, they travel by transformation through all lands;
with reverence and joy, they return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
If a person lacks roots of goodness, they shall not hear this sutra.
Those who possess pure precepts shall be able to hear the True Dharma.
Having once beheld the World-Honored One, they can believe in this matter;
hearing it with humility and reverence, they will practice it and leap for great joy.
Those plagued by pride and indolence find it difficult to believe in this Dharma;
those who have seen various Buddhas in past lives delight in hearing such teachings.
Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, none are able to fathom the Sage’s mind.
It is like one born blind who wishes to lead others along a path.
The ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is deep and vast, without shore or bottom;
it cannot be fathomed by those of the two vehicles, for only the Buddha alone understands it clearly.
Even if all people were to fully attain the Way,
their pure wisdom being like original emptiness, and were to contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom for billions of eons,
exhausting their strength and speaking to the utmost— yet even at the end of their lives they would still not know it.
The Buddha’s wisdom is boundless; thus he has attained purity.
A long life is extremely difficult to obtain, and a Buddha’s appearance in the world is likewise rare.
It is difficult for a person to possess both faith and wisdom; yet if one hears this, they should seek it with diligence.
One who hears the Dharma can never forget it; seeing and honoring it brings great joy.
Such a one is my true and virtuous friend; therefore, you should resolve your mind [to hear it].
Even if the entire world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma.
"They shall surely attain the Buddha-way and extensively deliver those in the flow of birth and death.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The bodhisattvas in that land shall all ultimately reach the stage of being 'one life remaining' before Buddhahood—except for those who, by their original vow, remain for the sake of sentient beings—and they adorn themselves with the merit of their great vows, universally desiring to liberate all sentient beings."
Ānanda! In that Buddha-land, the light from the bodies of the śrāvakas extends for one fathom, while the radiance of the bodhisattvas illuminates a hundred yojanas.
There are two bodhisattvas who are most honored and foremost; their majestic spiritual power and radiance shine universally throughout the trichiliocosm.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha,
“What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?
The Buddha said:
"The first is named Avalokiteśvara and the second is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
These two Bodhisattvas cultivated the bodhisattva practices in this land; at the end of their lives, they were transformed and reborn in that Buddha-land."

Ānanda! Those beings who are born in that land are all fully endowed with the thirty-two marks; their wisdom is perfected, they penetrate deeply into all dharmas, they exhaustively master the essential subtleties, their supernormal powers are unimpeded, and their faculties are clear and sharp.

Those of dull faculties accomplish the two types of patience (*kṣānti*), while those of sharp faculties attain the incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Furthermore, from that point until their attainment of Buddhahood, those bodhisattvas will no longer fall into the evil destinies; they possess mastery of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and always remember their past lives. Except when they are born in other worlds of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) to manifest among them—just as in my own land—they do not undergo such births.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“The bodhisattvas of that land, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, travel in a single mealtime to immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions to reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. According to their mental inclinations, countless and measureless articles for offering—such as flowers, incense, music, silken canopies, banners, and streamers—spontaneously manifest. These arrive instantly upon thought; they are precious, wondrous, and extraordinary, unlike anything found in this world.”

They were then further offered and scattered before the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of Śrāvakas; in the void they transformed into flower canopies, their radiant colors dazzling and their fragrance wafting everywhere.
The flowers that were four hundred li in circumference increased in size by double each time until they covered the trichiliocosm, appearing and then vanishing in succession according to their order.

All those bodhisattvas were filled with joy; together in the void, they played celestial music and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues with subtle and exquisite tones. Hearing and receiving the Dharma of the sutra, their joy was immeasurable.
After making offerings to the Buddha and before eating, he suddenly ascended lightly and returned to his own land.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"When Amitāyus Buddha proclaims the Dharma for the great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, they all gather in the lecture hall of the seven treasures.
