He extensively proclaims the Way and its teachings and expounds the wondrous Dharma; there are none who do not rejoice, whose minds are liberated, and who attain the Way."

Immediately, winds arose spontaneously from the four directions, blowing universally upon the jeweled trees to produce the five musical tones; immeasurable exquisite flowers rained down, circulating everywhere with the wind, providing spontaneous offerings that continued thus without ceasing.

All the devas brought hundreds of thousands of celestial flowers and incenses, as well as ten thousand kinds of musical performances, to make offerings to that Buddha, the bodhisattvas, and the great assembly of śrāvakas; they scattered flowers and incense everywhere, played various musical instruments, and moved back and forth, yielding to one another as they passed.
At that time, there was a radiant joy beyond words.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The bodhisattvas born in that buddha-land always proclaim the True Dharma in their discourses; they accord with wisdom, being neither contradictory nor erring."

Regarding all things within that land, they have no sense of "mine" and no mind of attachment; whether coming or going, advancing or stopping, their minds are free from entanglement. They act with spontaneous ease, without preference for one thing over another; there is neither "other" nor "self," and neither competition nor litigation.

Toward all sentient beings, they attain a mind of great compassion and benefit; a mind that is supple and disciplined, free from anger and resentment; a pure mind free from hindrances, weariness, and indolence; a mind of equanimity, a superior mind, a profound mind, and a concentrated mind; a mind that loves, delights in, and rejoices in the Dharma; and a mind that extinguishes all afflictions and leaves behind the evil realms. They bring to ultimate completion all the practices of Bodhisattvas, fully accomplishing immeasurable merits. They attain deep meditative concentrations, the various supernormal powers, and clear wisdom. Their resolve ranges through the seven factors of enlightenment as they cultivate the Buddha-dharmas. Their physical eye is so transparent that there is nothing it does not discern; their divine eye penetrates the infinite and the boundless; their Dharma-eye observes the ultimate nature of all paths; their wisdom-eye perceives the truth and is able to cross to the other shore; and their Buddha-eye is fully perfected in its awakening to the nature of phenomena.

Using unimpeded wisdom, they expound the Dharma for others; observing the three realms as equal, empty, and non-existent, they aspire to seek the Buddha-dharma and possess all eloquence to eliminate the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings.
Born from the Tathāgata, they understand that all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); they skillfully know the cessation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the expedient means of vocal expression.
They do not delight in worldly discourse but take pleasure in correct treatises; they cultivate the roots of all goodness, their resolve exalted toward the Buddha-way.
Knowing that all phenomena are entirely quiescent, the two remaining traces of the afflictions of the birth-body are both exhausted.
Hearing the profound Dharma, their minds feel no doubt or fear; they are those who can constantly practice great compassion.
Profound, far-reaching, and subtle, there is nothing it does not encompass; it brings the ultimate One Vehicle to the further shore.
It decisively cuts through the net of doubt, for wisdom emerges from the mind, comprehending all the Buddha’s teachings without exception.

His wisdom is like the great ocean and his samādhi is like the king of mountains; the radiance of his insight is pure and surpasses that of the sun and moon, and he is fully perfected in the dharmas of purity.
“Like the Snowy Mountains, because they illuminate all merits with equal purity;
like the great earth, because they harbor no discriminatory mind toward the pure and the defiled, or the good and the evil;
like pure water, because they wash away the defilements of worldly toil.”
They are like a king of fire, for they burn away and extinguish all the fuel of afflictions;
they are like a great wind, for they traverse all worlds without obstruction;
they are like space, for they are unattached to anything that exists.
It is like a lotus flower, for it is unstained by any worldly things;
it is like the Great Vehicle, for it carries all sentient beings across to transcend birth and death;
it is like a dense cloud, for it thunders the great Dharma-thunder to awaken those who have not yet awakened.
He is like a great rain, showering the Dharma of ambrosia to moisten all sentient beings;
he is like a mountain of vajra, which cannot be moved by any maras or non-Buddhists;
he is like Brahmā, the Lord of Gods, who is the foremost among all wholesome dharmas.
Like the nyagrodha tree, because it universally covers all;
like the udumbara flower, because it is rare and difficult to encounter;
like the garuḍa, because its majesty subdues the non-Buddhists.
Like a flock of migratory birds, because they possess no hoarded stores;
like a bull king, because none can surpass them;
like an elephant king, because they are well-tamed.
Like the lion king, because he is free from fear;
as vast as empty space, because his great compassion is impartial;
having crushed the mind of envy, because he does not hope for superiority.
He is single-mindedly devoted to seeking the Dharma, his mind never weary or satisfied;
he constantly desires to expound it widely, his resolve never faltering with fatigue.

He beats the drum of the Dharma, erects the banner of the Dharma, causes the sun of wisdom to shine, and dispels the darkness of ignorance. He cultivates the six points of harmonious respect, always practices the gift of Dharma, and maintains courageous diligence, his mind never retreating or weakening.
He is a lamp of light for the world and the most supreme field of merit; he constantly serves as a guide and teacher, equal toward all without hatred or affection.

Delighting only in the True Path, he has no other joys or sorrows; he plucks out the thorns of desire to bring peace to all living beings. His virtues are so preeminent that there are none who do not revere him; having extinguished the three defilements and obstructions, he wanders through the various supernormal powers.

They are fully endowed with all such powers as: the power of causes, the power of conditions, the power of intention, the power of vows, the power of skillful means, the power of constancy, the power of goodness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of extensive learning, the powers of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative absorption, and wisdom; the powers of right mindfulness, tranquility, insight, and the various supernormal knowledges and clarities; and the power to tame all sentient beings in accordance with the Dharma.
His physical form, color, and marks of excellence were adorned with the full perfection of merit and eloquence, such that none could equal him.
He had reverently made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and was constantly praised by all those Buddhas.

They bring the various *pāramitās* of the bodhisattvas to ultimate completion, cultivate the samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the various gateways of samādhi regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, and remain far removed from the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
“Ānanda! Those bodhisattvas have accomplished such immeasurable merits; I have merely spoken of them to you in brief.
Were they to be explained in detail, even hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas would not suffice to exhaust them.”
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, the devas, humans, and others:

"The merit and wisdom of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in the Land of Immeasurable Life are beyond description. Furthermore, since that land is so subtle, peaceful, blissful, and pure as this, why do you not strive to do good? Why not contemplate the spontaneity of the Way, abide in the state where there is neither high nor low, and penetrate to the boundless?"
"You should each apply yourselves with diligent vigor and strive to seek it for yourselves; you will surely attain transcendence and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
You shall cross through the five evil realms, which will naturally close;
you shall ascend the Path without end, yet few travel this easy way."

That land does not oppose or contradict [the truth], for it is naturally drawn toward it; why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice to seek the Way and its Virtue? Thus one may attain ultimate longevity, with a lifespan and bliss that have no end.
"Yet the people of this world are shallow and vulgar, contending over matters that are not urgent.
Amidst such extreme evil and intense suffering, they labor their bodies in worldly affairs merely to provide for themselves."

There is neither noble nor base, neither poor nor wealthy; young and old, male and female, all share equal anxiety over wealth and property; whether they possess it or lack it, their concerns are exactly the same.

Cowering in distress and suffering, with accumulated thoughts and persistent anxieties, one is driven like a servant by the mind, finding no moment of peace. One worries about fields if one has fields; one worries about houses if one has houses. Furthermore, one shares these concerns for cattle, horses, domestic animals, slaves, wealth, clothing, food, and household utensils. With heavy reflection and labored breathing, one is filled with anxiety, longing, and dread, as all things are suddenly consumed, swept away, plundered, or stolen by calamities, water, fire, thieves, enemies, or creditors; they vanish and are utterly destroyed. Thus, one is tormented by the poison of grief and trembling with fear, with no time of release.

Bound by resentment, his heart was never free from sorrow and affliction; his mind was firm and his will resolute, allowing no relaxation or abandonment. Eventually, while sitting, he was crushed to death and his life came to an end; as he was cast away and departed, there was no one who followed him.

“Noble and wealthy persons likewise have these afflictions; with myriad forms of anxiety and fear, their toil and suffering are such that they are accompanied by a multitude of chills, fevers, and pains.”

Poor, lowly, and destitute, they are constantly without anything; lacking fields, they grieve for having fields; lacking houses, they grieve for having houses; and lacking oxen, horses, livestock, slaves, wealth, clothing, food, and household utensils, they likewise grieve for having them.
Just as one thing is obtained, another is lost; what was possessed becomes diminished, and one longs for equality.
When one wishes to possess everything fully, it again dissolves and scatters.

Thus, amidst such sorrow and suffering, one must seek and search again, yet cannot obtain them in a timely manner. Such mental preoccupations are of no benefit; body and mind are both exhausted, one is restless whether sitting or rising, and anxious thoughts follow one another. With such diligent toil and hardship, one further contracts various chills and fevers, which coexist with physical pain.

At times, one may sit [in this state] until the end of life and meet an untimely death; being unwilling to do good, practice the Way, or advance in virtue, when life ends and the body dies, one must depart alone into the distance, heading toward either the path of goodness or evil—none can know where they will go.

"The people of the world—fathers and sons, brothers, husbands and wives, members of the household, and relatives both near and distant—should respect and love one another, never harboring hatred or envy.
They should share what they have with those who lack, never being greedy or stingy.
Their speech and countenances should always be harmonious; let there be no mutual opposition or conflict."

At times, when the mind is in conflict and harbors anger, a subtle sense of resentment and envy arises in this life, which grows increasingly severe in future lives until it becomes a great enmity. Why is this so?

Matters in the world involve mutual injury and harm; although they may not immediately result in instant destruction, the poison remains contained and the anger and resentment are stored within the spirit, naturally taking root in consciousness so that one cannot be separated from it. Thus, all must encounter rebirth and exact retribution upon one another.

In this world, amidst the midst of sensual desires, a person is born alone and dies alone; they go alone and come alone. When one must travel to the realms of suffering or happiness, one must experience it oneself, for there is no substitute.
The transformations of good and evil, and the divergent destinies of calamity and fortune, await one’s arrival with prior preparation; one must enter there alone.
Reaching far into another realm where none can see, good and evil naturally follow the one into their place of rebirth.
In the profound darkness of long-lasting separation, our paths diverge and the time for reunion is uncertain; it is most difficult, indeed most difficult, to encounter one another again.

Why not cast aside all worldly affairs while each of you is still vigorous and strong? Exert yourselves to diligently cultivate goodness and strive with vigor to transcend the world; thus may you attain ultimate longevity.
"How is it that you do not seek the Way? What do you wait for, and what do you desire to enjoy?

"In this way, the people of the world do not believe that performing good deeds brings good results or that practicing the Way leads to the Way. They do not believe in rebirth after death or that meritorious giving brings blessings. They do not believe in matters of good and evil at all, claiming they are otherwise and that such things simply do not exist."
It is solely because of this that they see only themselves; as they gaze upon one another, it is the same for all, whether senior or junior.

They merely inherit the remaining instructions of their fathers, yet their ancestors and grandfathers were fundamentally unvirtuous and ignorant of the Way and its Virtue; their persons were foolish and their spirits dark, their minds obstructed and their intentions closed.
One cannot perceive for oneself the destinations of birth and death or the paths of good and evil, nor is there anyone to speak of them;
yet, regarding fortune and misfortune, calamity and blessing, each person competes to create their own, with not a single instance of anything strange.

In the constant cycle of birth and death, beings succeed one another; sometimes the father weeps for the son, and sometimes the son weeps for the father. Brothers and spouses likewise weep for one another; with the inversion of high and low, there is no permanent foundation, for all must pass away and cannot be preserved forever.
When they are instructed and guided by my teachings, those who believe are few; thus, they wander through the cycle of birth and death without cessation.
Such people are ignorant and obstinate, disbelieving in the sutras and the Dharma; their minds lack foresight, and each seeks only their own gratification.
They are deluded by craving and desire, failing to comprehend the Way and its Virtue.
Bewildered and submerged in anger, greedily coveting wealth and beauty;
sitting thus, one fails to attain the Way and shall instead undergo the sufferings of the evil realms. Birth and death continue without end—alas, how deeply pitiable!

Sometimes within a household, fathers and sons, brothers, or husbands and wives—whether one has died or the other lives—mutually feel compassion; bound by affection, longing, and anxious concern, their minds are pained and deeply attached as they gaze upon one another with mutual yearning, exhausting the day and passing the year without ever finding release.
Though taught the words of morality, their minds remain unenlightened; though they contemplate kindness and goodness, they cannot part from sensual desires.

Clouded and obstructed, shrouded by ignorance and delusion, they are unable to reflect deeply or deliberate maturely, nor can they rectify their own minds, apply themselves single-mindedly to the Path, or decisively sever worldly affairs. Thus, as their lives eventually reach their end, they fail to attain the Way, left with no recourse.

"In general, all that is vulgar, chaotic, and disturbing arises from craving and desire; those who are deluded by the Way are many, while those who awaken to it are few. The world is in a state of frantic haste, with nothing upon which one can rely."

Whether high or low, superior or inferior, rich or poor, noble or base, those who toil and rush about in their affairs each harbor the poison of killing. Their evil vapors are dark and obscure as they recklessly give rise to matters that oppose heaven and earth and do not follow the human heart; thus, natural non-virtue spontaneously follows and accompanies them.
They will be allowed to act as they please until their transgressions reach their limit; yet, before their lifespan has even ended, they shall be suddenly seized and cast down into the evil realms.
There they shall endure accumulated resentment and suffering, revolving within them for thousands of billions of kalpas without any prospect of escape.
"The pain is beyond words; it is truly pitiable.
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, the devas, humans, and others:
"I now speak to you of worldly matters; it is because of these that people sit [in meditation] yet fail to attain the Way."
One should reflect deeply and plan to distance oneself from all evils, and having selected what is wholesome, practice it with diligence.
Love, desire, glory, and splendor cannot be maintained forever; one must inevitably part from them all, and therein is nothing to be enjoyed.

While the Buddha is in the world, you must exert yourselves with diligent vigor. Those who harbor the supreme aspiration to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss shall attain wisdom that is clear and penetrating, as well as preeminent merit and virtue;
do not follow your own whims, nor fail the sutras and precepts by falling behind others.
"If there are those who harbor doubts or fail to understand the sutra, they may inquire of the Buddha in full detail, and I shall explain it for them.
Maitreya Bodhisattva knelt with his right knee on the ground and said:
"The Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is most venerable, and what he has spoken is excellent and sublime; those who listen to the Buddha’s sutras contemplate it with focused minds."

The people of the world are indeed as the Buddha has said; now that the Buddha, out of compassion, has revealed the Great Way, their ears and eyes are opened and enlightened, and they shall forever attain liberation. Upon hearing what the Buddha has spoken, there are none who do not rejoice.
The devas, human beings, and even the crawling insects all receive his compassionate grace and are liberated from sorrow and suffering.

The Buddha’s words of instruction are profoundly deep and exceedingly good; with wisdom that clearly perceives the eight directions, above and below, and all matters of the past, future, and present, there is nothing he does not thoroughly understand and elucidate.
That we, this multitude, have now been granted deliverance is entirely due to the humility and asceticism practiced by the Buddha during his pursuit of the Way in previous lives.
His benevolent virtue covers all universally; his merit and fortune are towering and majestic; his radiance shines through, penetrating to the infinite void;

he opens the way for entry into Nirvana, and his teachings, which encompass and master all things, transform and dissolve [afflictions], moving those throughout the ten directions boundlessly and infinitely.
The Buddha is the Honored Dharma King who transcends all sages; he is the teacher of all devas and humans, causing them to attain the Way according to their heart's wishes.
Now that they have encountered the Buddha and heard the voice of Amitāyus, there are none who do not rejoice, and their minds are opened and enlightened.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"What you say is correct.
If there are those who possess loving-kindness and reverence for the Buddha, it is truly a great good."

Throughout the long course of time in this world, a Buddha appears but rarely; now, I have become a Buddha in this world to expound the sutras and the Dharma, proclaim the Way and its teachings, and sever the net of all doubts;
I uproot the foundation of craving and desire, and block the source of all evils.

He wanders through the three realms without obstruction, masterfully grasping the essentials of wisdom and the various paths; he maintains the guiding principles with clarity and precision, revealing the five destinies to deliver those not yet delivered, and decisively establishing the path between birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*.

“Maitreya, you should know that since you began practicing the bodhisattva path countless kalpas ago with the desire to deliver sentient beings, a vast period of time has passed; from the moment you attained the Way until your entry into nirvana, the number of those delivered is beyond calculation.”

You, along with all the devas, humans, and the fourfold assembly of the ten directions, have transmigrated through the five realms of existence since time immemorial; the anxieties, fears, and arduous sufferings you have endured cannot be fully described. Even until this present life, the cycle of birth and death has not ceased. Yet now, you have encountered the Buddha to hear and receive the Dharma, and furthermore, you have heard of the Buddha of Infinite Life.
"How wonderful! How excellent! I join you in your joy.

You too should now grow weary of birth, death, old age, sickness, suffering, impurities, and uncleanness—all of which are devoid of anything worth delighting in—and you ought to resolve this for yourself."
Maintain an upright body and correct conduct, further performing all manner of wholesome deeds;
cultivate oneself and purify the person, washing away the defilements of the mind;
let speech and action be loyal and trustworthy, so that the inner and outer correspond.
If a person can deliver themselves and, in turn, rescue others;

if they cultivate their clarity and vigor while seeking their vows and accumulating roots of goodness—then though they undergo diligent toil for but a moment in this life, in a future existence they shall be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where their happiness is infinite. There, they shall forever be united with the brilliance of the Way and its Virtue, eternally uprooting the very foundation of birth and death, and no longer suffer the afflictions of greed, anger, ignorance, or distress.

If one wishes for a lifespan of one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or ten trillion kalpas, one may attain it at will with sovereign ease; this state of non-action and spontaneity follows closely upon the path of Nirvana.

"You all should each apply yourselves with diligence to seek what your hearts desire; do not harbor doubts or regret, thereby bringing blame upon yourselves, lest you be born in those frontier lands within seven-jeweled palaces and suffer various calamities for five hundred years."
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Having received the Buddha’s grave instruction, I shall apply myself with single-minded diligence to cultivation and study, following and practicing according to your teaching, not daring to harbor any doubt.
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"If you are able, in this world, to maintain an upright mind and correct intention, refraining from all evil deeds, this is a most supreme virtue, peerless throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
Why is this? In the lands of the various Buddhas, the classes of devas and humans naturally perform good deeds and do not commit great evils; they are easily transformed and enlightened.
Now, I have become a Buddha in this world, dwelling amidst the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, which constitute the most intense suffering.
He transforms and instructs all living beings, causing them to abandon the five evils, eliminate the five pains, and distance themselves from the five burnings;

he subdues and transforms their minds, causing them to uphold the five virtues, so that they may attain merit and virtue and reach the path of Nirvana, which transcends the world and grants long life.
The Buddha said:
"What are the five evils?
What are the five sufferings?"
What are the five burnings?
What are the five evils that, when digested, cause one to uphold the five virtues, obtain their merit and fortune, and attain the path of Nirvana—transcending the world and attaining long life?
"Among those who are evil are the devas, human beings, and even the crawling insects.
There is none among them who does not desire to commit various evils.

The strong subdue the weak, mutually attacking and harming one another; they injure, slaughter, and devour each other in turn. They do not know to cultivate goodness, but instead act with malice and transgress the Way; consequently, they naturally head toward retribution and punishment."

The divine spirits record those who transgress and do not pardon them; consequently, there are those who are impoverished, lowly, beggars, solitary, deaf, blind, mute, dull-witted, or malicious, even reaching the point of being physically infirm, insane, or incapable.

Furthermore, those who possess nobility, great wealth, high talent, and clear discernment all do so because they practiced compassion and filial piety, cultivated goodness, and accumulated merit in past lives.

In this world, there are established norms, royal laws, and prisons; yet some are unwilling to be cautious or fearful. Committing evil, they fall into crime and receive its calamitous punishments, making it difficult for them to seek liberation or escape their fate.

In this world, there are such manifest matters before our eyes; after the end of one’s life, the consequences in future lives are even deeper and more severe, as one enters the dark realms to undergo rebirth and receive a new body.

It is like the agonizing and ultimate punishments of royal law; thus, there are the three miserable paths (*tāvatṛṣṇa*) with immeasurable suffering, where one exchanges one body for another and alters one's form and destiny. The lifespan received may be long or short, and the soul, spirit, and consciousness naturally gravitate toward them.

When they encounter one another and are born together, they continue to inflict harm upon each other without end; as their calamities and evils are not yet exhausted, they cannot separate from one another. They revolve within this state with no time of escape, and liberation is difficult to attain—their suffering is beyond words.
Between heaven and earth, this exists naturally; although its retribution may not arrive immediately or with sudden violence, the way of good and evil must inevitably lead back to it.
This constitutes one great evil, one great pain, and one great burning; such is the nature of diligent suffering.

“Suppose, for example, a great fire were to burn a person’s body; if one can therein single-mindedly restrain the will, maintain upright conduct, and alone perform all that is good while committing no evil, that person alone shall attain liberation, obtain merit, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the path of Nirvana—this is the first great goodness.”
The Buddha said:
"As for those two evils, the people of the world—fathers and sons, brothers, family members, and husbands and wives—all lack righteousness and do not accord with the laws and regulations."
Luxurious, lewd, arrogant, and self-indulgent, each seeking to gratify their own desires, they act according to their whims and indulge themselves, deceiving and deluding one another.

Their hearts and mouths differ; their words and thoughts lack sincerity. Deceitful and flattering, they are disloyal; with clever speech and sycophancy, they envy the worthy and slander the good, falling into grievous injustice.

The Sovereign lacks clarity in appointing his ministers; the ministers act with autonomy, employing manifold stratagems and deceptions. They tread upon the proper measures yet claim to carry out their duties, knowing only how to gauge the situation.
Their positions are not upright, and they are deceived by those they serve; they recklessly harm the loyal and virtuous, which does not accord with the Will of Heaven.

Ministers deceive their sovereigns and sons deceive their fathers; brothers, spouses, and those known from within and without families likewise deceive one another. Each harbors greed, anger, and delusion, desiring to enrich themselves and craving abundance; among the noble and the humble, the high and the low, all share this same state of mind.
They ruin their families and bring about their own destruction, heedless of consequences past or future; they cause their relatives, both near and distant, to perish along with them.

At times, entire households, acquaintances, local communities, market towns, ignorant commoners, and country folk join together in these activities, mutually stripping and harming one another until their anger forms a knot of resentment.

Though possessing wealth, one is stingy and unwilling to give; out of love for and greed for what one guards, the mind is weary and the body suffers. Thus, until the very end, there is nothing to rely upon; one comes alone and goes alone, with not a single follower.

Good and evil, calamity and fortune, follow one's life as it is born; whether one dwells in a place of joy or enters into bitter suffering, only then does one feel regret—by that time, what can possibly be done?

The people of the world are foolish in mind and deficient in wisdom; seeing what is good, they harbor hatred and slander rather than aspiring toward it. They desire only to do evil and recklessly commit unrighteous acts; constantly harboring thieving hearts, they covet the gains of others, exhausting and wearing themselves out in their pursuit until they must seek yet more.
With a deviant mind and lacking rectitude, one fears the disapproval of others; failing to deliberate and plan in advance, one only regrets when the matter arrives.
In this present world, there exist the laws of kings and prisons, through which one undergoes calamities and punishments according to the direction of one's offenses.

Because in their previous lives they did not believe in the Way and its Virtue and failed to cultivate the roots of goodness, yet now again commit evil, the celestial deities distinguish and record their names in the registers; when their lives end and their spirits depart, they descend into the evil realms, and thus there naturally arise the immeasurable sufferings of the three miserable paths.

Transmigrating within it, life after life through accumulated kalpas, there is no time of emergence; liberation is difficult to attain and its pain is unspeakable. These are the two great evils, the two pains, and the two burnings; such is the nature of this diligent suffering.

“Suppose, for example, a great fire were to burn a person’s body; if one can therein single-mindedly restrain the will, align the body, and rectify conduct, performing only various good deeds and committing no evils, that person alone shall attain liberation, obtain merit and virtue, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the path of Nirvana—this constitutes the second great goodness.”
The Buddha said:

"As for those three evils, the people of the world depend upon one another for their existence, dwelling together within heaven and earth; yet the duration of their years and lifespan is but a mere trifle."

Above are virtuous and wise elders, noble and wealthy; below are the poor, lowly, and wretched, as well as the weak and foolish. In between are those of unwholesome character who constantly harbor evil intentions; they think only of lewdness, which fills their chests with agitation. Their desires and passions are in turmoil, making them restless whether sitting or rising; with greedy minds, they cling to what they possess and seek only to obtain things for nothing.

He casts sidelong glances at subtle beauty, his licentious demeanor overflowing outwardly; he grows weary of and loathes his own wife, engaging in illicit and arbitrary outings; he squanders family wealth in unlawful acts, consorting with others in gatherings to raise armies for mutual assault, attacking, plundering, slaughtering, and seizing by force in a manner contrary to the Way.

With an evil mind directed outward, they do not cultivate their own practice; they resort to theft to obtain what they desire, seeking to accomplish their aims by intimidation and force, and fearing threats, they provide for their wives and children, indulging their hearts in pleasure and exhausting their bodies in sensual enjoyment.

Or, regarding their kinsmen, they disregard the distinction between the honorable and the humble; within and without the household, they cause them distress and suffering, and furthermore, they do not fear the prohibitions of the royal law.

Such evils become manifest to both humans and spirits; the sun and moon behold them, and the divine spirits record them. Consequently, there are naturally the immeasurable sufferings of the three miserable realms.

Transmigrating through these realms, life after life for countless eons, there is no time of escape; liberation is difficult to attain and the suffering is beyond description. These are the three great evils, the three pains, and the three burnings; such is the nature of their diligent toil and suffering.

“Suppose, for example, a great fire burns a person’s body; if one can therein single-mindedly restrain the will, maintain upright conduct, and alone perform all that is good while committing no evil, that person alone shall attain liberation, obtain merit, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the path of Nirvana—this is the third great goodness.”
The Buddha said, “As for those four evils, the people of the world do not think to cultivate goodness, but instead teach one another to commit various misdeeds together.

They engage in divisive speech, harsh speech, lying, and frivolous chatter; they slander and incite strife, harboring malice toward virtuous people and destroying the wise, while taking pleasure in such behavior.”
They are unfilial toward their two parents and disrespectful toward their teachers and elders; they lack integrity with friends and find it difficult to be sincere.

Arrogant and conceited because they believe themselves to possess the Way, they act with reckless authority, encroaching upon and exploiting others. Unable to know themselves, they commit evils without shame, and being self-satisfied in their own strength and vigor, they demand respect and reverence from others. Fearing neither Heaven and Earth, nor the divine spirits, nor the sun and moon, they refuse to do good and are difficult to transform or convert.
He treats himself with arrogance, believing that things may always remain as they are; he has no anxiety or fear, and constantly harbors conceit.

Because of such manifold evils, the heavenly deities take note of him. Relying on the fact that in his previous lives he performed some merit and virtue, minor wholesome deeds supported, sustained, and protected him;

yet now, having committed evil in this life, his merit and virtue are exhausted and extinguished. All the benevolent spirits and deities depart and leave him, so that he stands alone and empty, with nothing further upon which to rely.
When one's lifespan comes to an end, all evils converge upon them; naturally pressed and hurried, they are driven toward their own seizure.

Furthermore, their names are recorded in the registers of the divine spirits; dragged by their transgressions, they must proceed toward their destination, where the retribution for their sins occurs naturally, leaving no way to escape.
If one merely proceeds forward to enter the fiery cauldrons, with body and mind shattered and spirit in agony, what avail will repentance be at such a time?
The Way of Heaven is spontaneous and admits no deviation; thus there exist the three miserable realms of natural, immeasurable suffering and affliction.

Wandering through these realms, life after life for countless kalpas, there is no time of escape; liberation is difficult to attain and the suffering is beyond description. These are the four great evils, the four pains, and the four burnings; such is the nature of their diligent toil and hardship.

"Suppose, for example, that a great fire is burning a person's body; if one can therein single-mindedly restrain the will, keep the body upright and conduct correct, performing only various good deeds and committing no evils, so that the body alone attains liberation, secures its merit, and reaches the path of transcending the world, ascending to heaven, or attaining *nirvāṇa*—this is the fourth great good."
The Buddha said:

"As for those five evils, the people of the world are listless and indolent; they are unwilling to perform good deeds, discipline themselves, or cultivate their vocations, such that their families and kin suffer from hunger, cold, and hardship."

When parents offer instruction, they respond with glaring eyes and anger; their speech is discordant, and they act in opposition and rebellion like enemies. It would be better to have no child at all than such a one.
They take and give without moderation, causing universal weariness and resentment; they betray kindness and violate righteousness, lacking any heart of gratitude or recompense.

Being impoverished and destitute, they could no longer obtain [resources]; instead, they engaged in petty bargaining, seizing and plundering, and indulged in wanton dissipation. Habituated to such ways, they squandered their gains to provide for themselves.

They were addicted to wine and craved delicacies, eating and drinking without restraint; they gave rein to their hearts in licentiousness and idleness, acting with boorish insolence and aggression, showing no regard for human feelings while forcibly seeking to suppress others.
When seeing others possess virtue, they harbor hatred and envy toward it; lacking righteousness and propriety, they show no consideration or regard for others.

They are self-important and believe their own station is inviolable, refusing to be admonished or enlightened. They cannot even concern themselves with whether their own six close relatives and kin have the means to survive or not.

They disregard the kindness of their parents and fail to maintain the righteousness due to teachers and friends; their minds constantly harbor evil, their mouths constantly utter evil, and their bodies constantly perform evil, never having done a single good deed.

They do not believe in the sutras and teachings of the former sages and Buddhas; they do not believe that by practicing the Way one can attain deliverance from the world; they do not believe that after death the spirit and consciousness are reborn; and they do not believe that doing good brings good retribution while doing evil brings evil retribution.
They wish to kill true persons, to cause strife and disorder among the Sangha, and to harm their parents, brothers, and kinsmen; though their six relations loathe them, they wish for them to die.
"In this way, the minds of people in the world are likewise; though they are foolish and deluded, they imagine themselves to possess wisdom, not knowing whence birth comes or whither death leads."

Lacking benevolence and lacking compliance, they act in opposition to and malice toward Heaven and Earth; yet within this state, they harbor vain hopes and seek longevity, only to inevitably return to death.

Though they were instructed with a compassionate heart to mind what is wholesome, and shown that the destinies of birth and death—whether good or evil—naturally exist as such, the person did not believe it;
their bitter efforts and words were of no benefit to them, for their minds remained obstructed and their understanding failed to open.

When one’s great life is about to end, regret and fear arrive together; failing to cultivate goodness in advance and only feeling remorse when facing the ultimate limit—once regret comes too late, what can possibly be done?

Within heaven and earth, the five destinies are clearly distinguished; vast, profound, and boundless, they are immense and far-reaching. The retribution for good and evil and the succession of calamity and fortune follow one another; one must experience these oneself, for there is no one who can take one's place.
"The natural law of numbers responds to one's conduct; calamity and retribution pursue the life-force, allowing for no negligence or abandonment.
When good people perform good deeds, they proceed from joy to joy and from light to light;
when evil people perform evil deeds, they proceed from suffering to suffering and from darkness to darkness."
Who is able to know this?
Only the Buddha knows it alone.
Though he teaches and reveals it, those who believe and accept it are few; thus, birth and death do not cease, and the evil realms continue without end.
Thus, the world of men is difficult to fully describe; hence there are the three natural realms of suffering with immeasurable afflictions.

Wandering through them from life to life across kalpas, there is no time of escape, and liberation is hard to attain. The pain is beyond words; these are the five great evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, and such is the intensity of this diligent suffering.

“Suppose, for example, that a great fire is burning a person’s body; yet if one can within it single-mindedly restrain the will, keep the body upright with right mindfulness, ensure that words and deeds correspond, act with utmost sincerity, speak exactly as one thinks so that heart and mouth do not diverge, and practice only various virtues while committing no evils, then that person alone shall attain liberation, obtain merit, transcend the world, ascend to heaven, and reach the path of Nirvana—this is the fifth of the five great virtues.”
The Buddha told Maitreya: "I tell you all:

the hardships of the five evils in this world are such as these; the five pains and five burnings arise from one another in succession. Yet, by committing only various evils and failing to cultivate the roots of goodness, all naturally enter the various evil realms."

Or perhaps they have already been afflicted by calamity and disease in this present life, such that they cannot seek death nor can they seek life; thus the retribution summoned by their evil deeds is manifested for all to see.
When their bodies die, they follow their karma into the three evil realms, where they suffer immeasurable bitterness and poison, burning themselves from within.

After a long time, they formed a bond of enmity; what began as something minor eventually grew into great evil. All this arose from their greedy attachment to wealth and sensual pleasure, their inability to bestow wisdom, and their being driven by delusion and desire. Bound by the fetters of afflictions with no prospect of release, they were preoccupied with enriching themselves and contending for profit, showing no self-reflection.

Wealth, nobility, and splendor may bring momentary gratification, yet if one cannot endure insults and fails to cultivate goodness, such power and influence will soon vanish, leaving only physical toil and suffering that become increasingly severe over time.
The Way of Heaven is spread out and naturally enforces its regulations; its governing framework and netting correspond from top to bottom. Solitary and trembling, one must enter within it.
This has been so throughout antiquity and the present—how painful and tragic!
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
"The world is thus; the Buddha pities it all.

By means of his majestic spiritual power, he crushes and extinguishes all evils, causing everyone to turn toward goodness and abandon their worldly thoughts. They uphold the sutras and precepts, practice the Way and its teachings without transgression, and ultimately attain the path of nirvana that transcends the world."
The Buddha said:

"Now, you gods, humans, and those of future generations, upon encountering the words of the Buddha’s sutras, you should contemplate them deeply. You should be able to maintain an upright mind and practice correct conduct therein; as rulers, you should do good and lead and transform those below you, repeatedly exhorting one another to each maintain integrity and self-restraint, honoring the sages, revering the virtuous, and practicing benevolence and universal love."

One must not dare to violate or neglect the Buddha’s words and instructions; one should seek transcendence from the world and uproot the very source of all evils of birth and death, forever departing from the path of immeasurable anxiety, fear, and suffering within the three miserable realms.

You all should extensively plant the roots of merit, bestow kindness and wisdom, and do not violate the prohibitions of the Path; through patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, you should transform and instruct one another.

"To cultivate virtue and establish goodness, to rectify the heart and rectify the will, and to observe the fast with purity for one day and one night, is superior to practicing goodness for a hundred years in the Land of Immeasurable Life."

Why is this? That Buddha-land is unconditioned and spontaneous, where all manner of virtues have accumulated and not even a hair’s breadth of evil exists; to practice virtue here for ten days and ten nights surpasses practicing virtue for a thousand years in the lands of other Buddhas.
Why is this? Because in the Buddha-lands of other directions, those who do good are many and those who do evil are few; merit and virtue are spontaneous, and there is no ground for committing evil.

Only here is there much evil and nothing natural; one strives with hardship in pursuit of desires, deceiving and endangering one another. The mind is exhausted and the body is weary as one drinks bitterness and eats poison; thus, in this frantic bustle, there is never a moment of rest.

I pity you, beings of both celestial and human kind, and with a sincere heart I instruct and exhort you to cultivate goodness. According to your capacities, I guide you and bestow upon you the sutras and the Dharma; there are none who do not accept and apply them, and I cause all to attain the Way according to their aspirations.

Wherever the Buddha traveled—whether through kingdoms, cities, villages, or hamlets—all were transformed by his influence. The world became harmonious and compliant; the sun and moon shone with clarity; wind and rain fell in their proper seasons; calamities and pestilences did not arise; the state was prosperous and the people at peace; weapons of war were rendered useless; virtue was honored and benevolence promoted; and all applied themselves to the cultivation of ritual propriety and yielding.
The Buddha said:
"I have compassion for you, gods and humans alike, surpassing that of parents for their children.

Now that I have attained Buddhahood in this world, I subdue and transform the five evils, eliminate the five pains, and extinguish the five burnings. Using the good to overcome evil, I uproot the suffering of birth and death, enabling you to attain the five virtues and ascend to the peace of the unconditioned."

After my passing from this world, the Way and the teachings will gradually perish; the people will become deceitful and hypocritical, committing various evils once more. The five burnings and five pains will recur as they did before, and over time they will intensify beyond all description; I have merely spoken of them briefly for your sake.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“Each of you should contemplate this well and instruct one another; act in accordance with the Buddha’s sutras and teachings, and do not transgress them.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva joined his palms and said:
"What the Buddha has spoken is most excellent.

It is indeed so for the people of the world; the Tathāgata, with universal compassion and pity, causes all to be delivered and liberated. Having received the Buddha’s profound instruction, we dare not disobey or err."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Rise, adjust your robes once more, join your palms in reverence, and pay homage to the Buddha Amitāyus.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, throughout the lands of the ten directions constantly extol and praise that Buddha, who is unattached and unimpeded."

Thereupon, Ānanda rose, adjusted his robes, straightened his body facing west, joined his palms in reverence, and prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to Amitāyus Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that I may behold that Buddha’s Land of Peace and Bliss, as well as its assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas."

When these words had been spoken, the Buddha of Infinite Life immediately emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated all Buddha-worlds; the Diamond Rim Mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and all mountains, great and small—everything that exists—became of one single color.
For example, when the waters of the kalpa flood the world, all things therein are submerged and no longer appear; vast and boundless, one sees only the great water.
The radiance of that Buddha is likewise: the light of all śrāvakas and bodhisattvas is entirely eclipsed, and one sees only the Buddha’s radiance shining with brilliant splendor.

At that time, Ānanda immediately beheld Amitāyus Buddha, whose majestic virtue was as towering as Mount Sumeru, rising high above all the worlds, with his primary and secondary marks and radiant light illuminating everything without exception.
The fourfold assembly in this gathering all saw that land at once, and those there saw this land in the same way.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda and the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Do you see that land, from the ground upward to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and all the subtle, wondrous, pure, and spontaneous things therein? Do you see them all?"
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, I have seen it. [The Buddha asked:
“Do you also hear the great voice of Amitāyus Buddha proclaiming throughout all worlds to transform sentient beings?”
Ānanda replied, "Indeed, I have heard it. [The Buddha said:

"Do you also see how the people of that land, riding in palaces made of the seven treasures and measuring hundreds of thousands of yojanas, travel everywhere throughout the ten directions without obstruction to make offerings to the Buddhas?"
He replied, “I have seen them. [The Buddha asked:
“Among the people of that land, are there any who are born from a womb? Have you seen them as well?”
He replied, "I have seen them.

[The Buddha asked,] "As for those born from the womb, the palaces where they dwell are either one hundred yojanas or five hundred yojanas in extent; within each of these, they experience various pleasures just like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, all of which arise spontaneously."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition do the people of that land undergo birth from a womb or miraculous birth?”
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land, yet do not understand the Buddha’s wisdom—the inconceivable wisdom, the incomparable wisdom, the vast Mahāyāna wisdom, and the peerless, supreme, and most excellent wisdom—and harbor doubts and lack faith in these various forms of wisdom;
nevertheless, they still believe in the retribution of sin and merit, cultivate the roots of goodness, and vow to be born in that land."

These beings born in that palace have a lifespan of five hundred years; they constantly do not see the Buddha, do not hear the sutras and Dharma, and do not see the assembly of bodhisattvas and noble śrāvakas. For this reason, birth in that land is called "womb-birth" (garbhaja).

If there are sentient beings who clearly believe in the Buddha’s wisdom, even up to his supreme wisdom, and who perform various meritorious deeds with a faithful mind and dedicate them toward enlightenment, these beings will be spontaneously born by transformation within lotus flowers made of the seven treasures, sitting cross-legged. In a mere moment, their physical marks and radiance, as well as their wisdom and merit, will be fully perfected, just like those of the bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
Great Bodhisattvas from other directions resolve to see Amitāyus Buddha, and to reverently make offerings to him as well as to the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas."

Those bodhisattvas, at the end of their lives, will attain rebirth in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where they will be spontaneously born by transformation within flowers made of the seven precious substances.
Maitreya, you should know that those who are so born by transformation possess superior wisdom.

Those born from a womb all lack wisdom; for five hundred years they constantly fail to see the Buddha, hear the sutras and the Dharma, or encounter the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Having no means to make offerings to the Buddha, they do not know the regulations of the bodhisattvas and cannot cultivate merit. One should know that this person lacked wisdom in their past lives, which resulted from the influence of doubt.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"It is, for example, as if a Wheel-Turning Sage King had a separate palace adorned with the seven treasures, where couches and canopies were spread and silken banners were suspended."

If any minor princes commit an offense against the king, he immediately takes them into his inner palace and binds them with golden chains; yet he provides them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, flowers, incense, and music, so that they lack for nothing, just like the Universal Monarch.
"What do you think?
Would these princes find pleasure in that place?
He replied:
"No, they merely employ various skillful means to seek great strength, desiring to exert themselves and emerge.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"These sentient beings are just like this."

Because they harbored doubts regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, they were born in that palace; there, they are subject to neither punishment nor even a single moment of evil, yet for five hundred years they do not see the Triple Gem, nor can they make offerings or cultivate the roots of all virtues.
Regarding this as suffering, even if there were other pleasures, one would still find no joy in that place.

If these sentient beings recognize their original transgressions, deeply repent and reproach themselves, and seek to leave that place, they will immediately attain their wish: they shall go to the abode of Amitāyus Buddha to pay respectful homage and make offerings, and they shall also be able to reach the presence of immeasurable and innumerable Tathāgatas to cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues.
Maitreya, you should know that any bodhisattva who gives rise to doubt will lose a great benefit.
Therefore, one should clearly believe in the unsurpassed wisdom of all Buddhas.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many non-retrogressive bodhisattvas in this world will be born in that buddha-land?”
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In this world, there are sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land.
Each and every one of these bodhisattvas has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, and each is equal to you, Maitreya."
"Incalculable numbers of bodhisattvas who have performed minor practices and those who have cultivated few merits shall all be reborn there.
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"It is not only the bodhisattvas of my own land who will be reborn in that country; it is likewise so for those from the buddha-lands of other directions."
The first Buddha is named Dūraprabha; one hundred and eighty billion bodhisattvas from that realm shall all be reborn there.
The second Buddha is named Ratnagarbha; ninety billion bodhisattvas from that realm shall all be reborn there.
The third Buddha is named Immeasurable Sound; two hundred and twenty billion bodhisattvas from there shall all be reborn there.
The fourth Buddha is named Ambrosial Flavor; two hundred and fifty billion bodhisattvas from there shall all be reborn there.
The fifth Buddha is named Dragon Victor (Nāgajaya); fourteen hundred million bodhisattvas from his realm shall all be reborn there.
The sixth Buddha is named Supreme Power (Jinabala); fourteen thousand bodhisattvas from his realm shall all be reborn there.
The seventh Buddha is named Siṃha; five hundred billion bodhisattvas from his realm shall all be reborn there.
The eighth Buddha is named Vimalaprabha; eight billion bodhisattvas from his realm shall all be reborn there.
The ninth Buddha is named Virtue Chief; sixty billion bodhisattvas from his realm shall all be reborn there.
The tenth Buddha is named Wondrous Virtue Mountain; sixty billion bodhisattvas from his realm shall all be reborn there.
The eleventh Buddha is named King of Men; ten billion bodhisattvas shall all be reborn there.

The twelfth Buddha is named Supreme Flower; he has an immeasurable and incalculable multitude of bodhisattvas—all of whom are non-retrogressive, possessed of courageous wisdom, and have already made offerings to countless Buddhas. Within seven days, they are able to grasp the firm dharmas practiced by great beings over hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas—all such bodhisattvas shall be reborn there.

The thirteenth Buddha is named Abhaya; he has a multitude of seven hundred and ninety billion great bodhisattvas, as well as innumerable minor bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and others, all of whom shall be reborn there.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

“It is not only the bodhisattvas in these fourteen buddha-fields who shall be reborn there; those who are reborn in the immeasurable buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions are likewise so numerous that they are beyond counting.”

If I were to speak only of the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions and of the bodhisattvas and bhikṣus born in that land, I would not finish even in a full day and night or an entire kalpa; I have now merely spoken of them briefly for you.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

"Should anyone hear the name of that Buddha and, with joyful exultation, even for a single thought-moment, you should know that this person has attained great benefit and is fully endowed with unsurpassed merit."
Therefore, Maitreya!
Even if a great fire were to fill the trichiliocosm, one must pass through it;
yet upon hearing this Dharma of the sutra, one should rejoice with faith and delight, receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice according to its teachings.
Why is this? There are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra but are unable to obtain it.
If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, they will never regress from the unsurpassed path; therefore, one should single-mindedly believe, accept, uphold, recite, explain, and practice it.

I now preach this Dharma of the sutra for the sake of all sentient beings, so that they may behold Amitāyus Buddha and everything within his land; whatever they ought to do, they may seek it therein, and let none harbor further doubt or confusion after my parinirvāṇa.

In a future age, when the Way of the sutras has been extinguished, out of compassion and pity I shall specially preserve this sutra so that it remains for a hundred years. Any sentient beings who encounter this sutra shall all attain liberation according to their wishes.
The Buddha said to Maitreya:
“The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter and difficult to behold; the sūtras and teachings of the Buddhas are difficult to obtain and difficult to hear;
and it is likewise difficult to hear the supreme dharmas of the Bodhisattvas, the various pāramitās.”
To encounter a virtuous friend and hear the Dharma such that one is able to practice it is already difficult;
yet, if upon hearing this sutra one can believe, rejoice in, accept, and uphold it, this is the most difficult of difficulties—nothing surpasses this difficulty.
"Therefore, my Dharma is thus enacted, thus proclaimed, and thus taught; you should believe and comply with it, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, as the World-Honored One preached this sutra and its Dharma, immeasurable sentient beings all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*); twelve thousand *nayutas* of people attained the pure Dharma-eye; twenty-two billion devas and humans attained the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin*); eight hundred thousand bhikṣus exhausted their outflows and attained liberation of mind; and four billion bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression, adorning themselves with the merit of great vows, destined to attain perfect enlightenment in a future age.

At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great light shone universally throughout the lands of the ten directions; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played spontaneously; and immeasurable, wondrous flowers fell in profusion.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions, the Elder Ānanda, the great śrāvakas, and the entire great multitude, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with joy.
